## Project summary

Core 4x4 is a real-world business analytics project centered on marketplace and internal sales data arriving in different export formats. The repository implements a local Windows application that turns those inputs into a standardized, traceable event ledger.

The workflow supports file-type detection, product and SKU mapping, exact-file and business-record duplicate handling, validation reports, optional SQL Server loading, and analytics views for Power BI. Proprietary records and business details are intentionally excluded from this public case study.

## Business problem

Sales information from separate platforms can differ in structure, naming conventions, product identifiers, and record quality. Without a consistent preparation process, those differences make it harder to combine records and use them reliably in reporting.

The project addresses the need for a shared analytical foundation: one that preserves the useful information in each source while applying common business rules before analysis.

## My role

I worked across the data-preparation workflow, including reviewing source structures, shaping Python transformation logic, standardizing fields, supporting product and SKU mapping, handling duplicate records, defining validation behavior, and preparing SQL and Power BI assets.

I also used Git and GitHub to manage and track the project code. Specific organizational details and proprietary data are intentionally omitted.

## Solution

The solution organizes the work into source adapters, a canonical event schema, shared validation and mapping rules, and controlled output steps. Users can process files through a local desktop or browser interface, review warnings, save a standardized CSV and validation report, and optionally load approved results into SQL Server for Power BI.

::: {.solution-callout}
### Design principle

Separate source-specific cleanup from shared business rules. This makes the workflow easier to reason about and extend when a source changes or a new one is introduced.
:::

## Key challenges

:::: {.challenge-grid}
::: {.challenge-card}
### Inconsistent source formats
Each source can represent similar business information differently. The workflow needs to preserve meaning while creating a consistent structure.
:::

::: {.challenge-card}
### Product identity
Product names and SKUs may not align cleanly across inputs. Mapping creates a common reference for downstream analysis.
:::

::: {.challenge-card}
### Duplicate records
Potential duplicates require explicit handling so that combined files do not quietly distort later reporting.
:::

::: {.challenge-card}
### Data validation
Transformations need checks that surface unexpected values or structural issues before the data reaches Power BI.
:::
::::

## Key features

- Source adapters for tested eBay and Core 4x4 exports
- Amazon-format adapter present but not yet validated with a real sample
- Automatic source detection with a manual selection fallback
- Canonical event ledger with source lineage and stable record keys
- Approved SKU mapping from XLSX or CSV files
- Exact-file and business-record duplicate handling
- Validation reports with warning and review-needed records
- Transactional SQL Server loading for approved runs
- SQL analytics views, Power BI measures, and automated tests

## Business value

The pipeline provides a more consistent foundation for sales analysis by making source differences, lineage, mapping rules, duplicate handling, and validation part of a repeatable process. The output can be reviewed as files before approved runs are stored for downstream reporting.

No quantitative performance or financial claims are included because those outcomes have not been established for publication.

## What I learned

This project reinforced that dependable analytics begins before a dashboard is built. Source context, naming conventions, product identity, and validation rules all shape whether an analytical output can be trusted.

It also highlighted the importance of designing workflows in stages. A modular process makes it easier to isolate issues, revise business rules, and communicate how raw information becomes a reporting dataset.

## Future improvements

The repository identifies Amazon sample validation and continued operational hardening as areas for future work. Additional improvements could extend automated quality checks and make the approved-load and Power BI refresh process easier to operate.
